Stories like stay at home mothers brought to court for a small handful of songs downloaded from Napster and fines hundreds of thousands of dollars or jail time for file sharing has remained in the minds of would be peer to peer users.

But if lack of knowledge about VPN's and torrent sites and the fear of persecution isn't enough, the sheer perception of the daunting difficulty to set up a VPN is enough to make the vast majority of people feel like forking over $10/mo is easier and acceptable. Putting it simple, people like convenience. They think a small subscription fee is no big deal.

Amazon pioneered the long tail sales strategy and companies have taken lesson and applied it in varying forms, most sinisterly seen in small monthly subscriptions. Now, our society is happily being slowly bled financially one dollar at a time. Subscriptions to online services have proliferated in the last decade from things like music and tv streaming subscriptions with Spotify, Pandora, and Netflix, to network data storage like iCloud, and online software like Adobe Creative Suite.

It's no surprise that Apple doesn't offer removable data storage and has even shrunk their phone's data storage capacity in many of their second tier models and even their budget version of their flag ship models. It's profitable to get people locked into cloud data storage. On one side, Apple gets more revenue per gigabyte over the time of an average two year cellular contract, and on the other side, the customer becomes locked into Apple's online cloud storage and iOS to preserve legacy (because who wants to give up on that precious data legacy).
